title: Claude Code Dynamic Workflows and CSM Skill Worker Architecture Research Finding

tldr.content: Claude Code dynamic workflows move runtime decomposition, fan-out, branching, intermediate results, and replay into an executable JavaScript harness, with a dedicated progress view for phases and agents. The closest safe analogue here is a shared bounded worker runtime at the csm-orchestrate layer, with each skill declaring its worker policy and result/gate contract. Progress must be a first-class redacted event stream plus materialized snapshot, not prose or a terminal receipt field.

executiveSummary.content:
This DEEP hybrid investigation combined five independent research tracks, direct current Anthropic documentation, a local inspection of the skill suite and runtime, an adversarial challenge, and two judge passes.

```text
user request
   -> model-authored workflow/control decision
   -> bounded worker runtime
      -> dynamic task/worker creation
      -> parallel isolated contexts
      -> typed results and barriers
      -> retry/replay/evaluator decisions
   -> event log -> live snapshot -> CLI/dashboard projection
   -> authoritative receipt and resumable cursor
```

Claude Code exposes several related mechanisms, not one monolithic feature: subagents isolate context and return results; dynamic workflows execute a script that owns loops and intermediate results; agent teams add a lead, peer messaging, and a shared task list; hooks provide lifecycle intervention; Agent View, workflow views, status lines, streaming, and OpenTelemetry provide different observability scopes. The local suite already has strong state machines, artifact lineage, approvals, gates, retries, and some adaptive decomposition guidance. Its key gap is runtime execution telemetry and dynamic worker/task state, while csm-orchestrate currently compiles a fixed approach and executes route nodes serially.

keyFindings.content:
K1 [supported] Claude Code dynamic workflows move orchestration into a JavaScript runtime that owns loops, branching, fan-out, and intermediate results, leaving the parent context with the final answer rather than every intermediate result. [ref-workflows]

K2 [supported] The dynamic behavior is a hybrid: Claude writes or adapts the workflow harness, while the runtime executes ordinary JavaScript and worker primitives such as `agent()`, `pipeline()`, arrays, filtering, and invocation arguments. [ref-workflows-script]

K3 [supported] Claude worker configuration is runtime-selectable: SDK subagent definitions can specify prompts, tools, models, permissions, maximum turns, effort, background behavior, skills, and other supported fields; definitions can also be created at query time. [ref-subagents-sdk]

K4 [supported] Dynamic execution is bounded outside the prompt by concurrency, total-agent, nesting-depth, turn, and spend controls. Workflow limits and SDK limits are version/configuration dependent and must be treated as policy inputs, not universal constants. [ref-workflow-limits][ref-agent-limits][ref-agent-loop]

K5 [supported] Claude Code provides a distinct progress surface for workflows: reported phases, agent counts, token totals, elapsed time, recent prompts/tool calls/results, and pause/stop/restart controls. These are observable activity and runtime controls, not proof of exact completion percentage or ETA. [ref-workflow-watch][ref-agent-view][ref-statusline]

K6 [supported] Workflow resume has replay semantics: unfinished agents may restart and agents started later in the fan-out may rerun. Side-effecting work therefore needs replay tolerance, idempotency, durable completion markers, or explicit at-least-once semantics; this last requirement is an architectural inference. [ref-workflow-resume]

K7 [supported] Subagent context isolation reduces parent-context growth but does not establish OS, process, filesystem, credential, or security isolation. Those boundaries need separate permission, sandbox, worktree, and persistence controls. [ref-subagents-sdk][ref-workflows][ref-agent-loop]

K8 [supported] Hooks and OpenTelemetry form complementary control and observability planes: hooks can intercept or alter operations and receive lifecycle callbacks, while OTel can correlate agents, parent agents, workflow runs, tool-use IDs, duration, success, and model requests. OTel is opt-in, tracing is beta/off by default in the documented configuration, and hooks are not themselves a redacted telemetry stream. [ref-hooks-sdk][ref-monitoring]

K9 [supported] In the inspected repository implementation, csm-orchestrate precompiles supplied approach phases, routes from a fixed capability manifest, invokes route nodes in a serial loop, awaits terminal child results, and has a trace-event constructor that was not found wired into a live callback or stream. [ref-orchestrate-contract][ref-orchestrate-runtime][ref-orchestrate-concurrency][ref-orchestrate-trace]

K10 [partially-supported] The skill suite has candidate skill-level ingredients for adaptive workers: csm-build has dependency-ready batching and ownership partitioning; csm-review has dimension/chunk assignment and severity-scaled challenge; csm-deep-research has tier-based expert sizing and role separation; csm-make-tests has gap-driven generation; csm-autoresearch has runtime populations, stagnation, migration, and evaluator-owned safety. Comparative superiority is not established, and worker allocation, worker health, and live event contracts are not first-class in the inspected schemas. [ref-build-select][ref-review-scaling][ref-research-triage][ref-tests-parallel][ref-autoresearch-population]

K11 [recommendation] Centralize bounded worker-runtime concerns in the orchestrator and let skills declare decomposition strategy, worker policy, result contract, gate policy, and milestone semantics. This is an architectural recommendation inferred from the evidence, not an Anthropic requirement. [ref-workflows][ref-agent-limits][ref-orchestrate-contract][ref-build-select]

K12 [recommendation] Implement progress as privacy-safe lifecycle events with stable run, phase, task, worker, invocation, and tool identifiers; persist an append-only event history and materialized current snapshot; render CLI/dashboard views from snapshots; keep cursors and terminal receipts authoritative; surface degraded durability and replay explicitly. This is a proposed design, not an observed Claude Code implementation requirement. [ref-hooks-sdk][ref-monitoring][ref-orchestrate-trace][ref-journal-schema]

detailSections.content:
### What dynamic workflows actually add

Claude Code's workflow documentation distinguishes the plan holder. A skill is instructions Claude follows; a subagent is a worker Claude spawns; an agent team is a lead supervising peer sessions; a workflow is a script the runtime executes. The important shift is not simply a larger fan-out. The script owns the control loop and keeps intermediate values out of the parent context. The documented script shape is intentionally small: a top-level `await`, `agent()` for one worker, `pipeline()` for one worker per item, ordinary JavaScript for classification/filtering, and `args` for structured invocation input.

The resulting control patterns are composable:

```text
classify -> route
              |
              +-> fan-out -> barrier -> synthesize
              +-> adversarial verify
              +-> generate -> filter/dedupe
              +-> tournament -> judge
              +-> loop until stop condition
```

Anthropic's broader guidance says fixed workflows are preferable when subtasks are known, while orchestrator-workers fit tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted. Autonomous loops are appropriate only when open-ended flexibility justifies higher cost and compounding-error risk. This argues for a mode switch, not a universal dynamic scheduler.

### Worker context, execution, and replay

The sources support fresh worker conversations and summarized/final result return, but context isolation must not be misrepresented as a security sandbox. A CSM worker contract should separately declare tool permissions, side effects, workspace/worktree, network policy, credential visibility, and artifact authority.

The workflow runtime tracks agent results and can resume within the same Claude Code session, but resume may restart unfinished work and replay later fan-out work. A safe CSM analogue should make delivery semantics explicit: at-least-once worker execution by default, deterministic `idempotencyKey` per logical task attempt, durable terminal marker, and a reconciliation path that prefers a verified terminal result over duplicate execution. A worker that was active at interruption should be visibly `restarted` or `replayed`, not silently counted as a fresh success.

### Local architecture and gap

The current orchestrator's contract is already a strong safety shell:

```text
canonical approach -> phase compiler -> fixed capability route
                                      |
                                      v
                         host invocation -> terminal child result
                                      |
                         artifact/evidence gates -> receipt
```

Its implementation requires an injected host and durable cursor store, binds approvals and child identities, validates artifact/evidence lineage, and requires technical, functional, and final review gates. However, the inspected loop iterates through precompiled phases and route nodes serially. The invocation adapter awaits a final child result and does not expose incremental worker events. The existing `csm-orchestrate-trace/1` object has correlation and free-form data, but its constructor was not found used as an emitted event stream. The generic `csm-journal-event/1` supports run, artifact, and delegation lifecycle types, but not worker/task start, progress, heartbeat, retry, cancellation, or tool events.

The local skill contracts reinforce this conclusion. `csm-build` describes selecting the largest safe dependency-ready batch and launching independent assignments concurrently, but its state schema records active task IDs rather than worker leases, heartbeats, capacity, or invocation telemetry. `csm-deep-research` scales panels by tier and separates synthesizer, challenger, judge, and verifier, but its durable contract is research-state and claim-oriented. `csm-autoresearch` is the most runtime-adaptive skill because its population and stagnation logic is explicit and machine-backed, but its unit of optimization is candidate evaluation rather than general-purpose worker execution.

### Progress model required for trustworthy visualization

Separate four concepts:

| Concept | Meaning | Safe UI representation | Not safe to infer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| State | lifecycle position | pending, running, blocked, retrying, completed, failed, cancelled, replayed | percentage complete |
| Activity | what the worker recently did | current phase, last bounded action, recent tool category, heartbeat age | correctness or remaining work |
| Progress | declared work completed | milestone/weight and verified fraction when the skill can measure it | ETA without a calibrated model |
| Evidence | what proves acceptance | artifact/evidence IDs, gate outcomes, receipt links | success from activity alone |

A minimum event vocabulary should include `run.started/completed/failed`, `phase.started/completed`, `task.created/ready/blocked/completed`, `worker.started/heartbeat/progress/retrying/completed/failed/cancelled/replayed`, `invocation.started/completed/failed`, `tool.started/completed/failed`, `artifact.created/verified`, and `checkpoint.saved`. Each event should carry a monotonic sequence, occurred time, run/phase/task/worker/invocation correlation, redacted bounded data, and an idempotency/event identity.

The event stream should be append-only and immutable; a snapshot materializer should fold events into current run, phase, task, worker, gate, and evidence rows. A CLI renderer can show an overall bar plus a worker table, while an HTML/dashboard projection can subscribe or poll snapshots. Event snapshots are operational observability; the authoritative state machine, cursor, artifact lineage, and terminal receipt remain acceptance authority.

### Layer placement

The recommended boundary is:

```text
Skill contract
  declares: decomposition, worker role, input/output schema, effects, permissions,
            retry/idempotency, gates, milestone weights, progress measurability
        |
        v
Shared worker runtime
  enforces: leases, capacity, concurrency, cancellation, timeout, retries,
            event emission, snapshotting, replay, redaction, lineage
        |
        v
Orchestrator
  decides: whether dynamic mode is warranted, which skill routes are allowed,
           barriers, approvals, final synthesis, final acceptance
```

Individual skills should not each implement a scheduler. They should expose policy and domain-specific callbacks/roles. The orchestrator should support fixed mode by default and a bounded dynamic mode only where a skill contract explicitly permits it. This preserves existing safety boundaries and makes dynamic behavior auditable.

recommendation.content:
Recommend a hybrid design, subject to repository-local validation before implementation:

1. Keep current fixed state machines, typed artifacts, approvals, evidence gates, terminal receipts, and durable cursors as the acceptance authority.
2. Add a shared worker-runtime contract beneath csm-orchestrate rather than duplicating scheduling logic in every skill.
3. Let each skill publish a versioned worker policy: permitted worker roles, decomposition mode, maximum fan-out, concurrency, depth, budget, timeout, tool/effect permissions, workspace isolation, result schema, retry/idempotency mode, gate obligations, and measurable milestones.
4. Permit dynamic mode only when the selected skill policy and route approval explicitly allow it. The model may propose tasks/workers, but runtime validation must enforce schema, capability, dependency, ownership, budget, and effect limits.
5. Start with bounded patterns that match existing skills: build ready-set fan-out, review dimension/chunk fan-out, research angle fan-out, test-gap fan-out, and autoresearch candidate populations. Add loop-until-done only with an explicit stop predicate and iteration budget.
6. Add a worker/event schema and event sink at the shared layer. Do not overload the existing free-form trace helper or terminal receipt with live state.
7. Materialize a live snapshot and render two views: an overall weighted milestone bar and a worker table showing state, activity, heartbeat age, attempt, model, token/cost data when available, and evidence/gate status. Mark unknown progress as unknown rather than fabricating percentages.
8. Make replay visible and safe. Use logical task IDs plus attempt IDs, durable completion markers, idempotency keys, duplicate-event handling, and explicit `replayed`/`degraded-durability` states.
9. Integrate hook-like lifecycle points around worker start/stop, task creation/completion, tool execution, checkpoint, and cancellation. Policy decisions must be deterministic and order-independent.
10. Treat workflow-style progress as operational visibility, not proof of correctness. The final result cannot become `VERIFIED` until existing artifact, technical, functional, adversarial, and review gates pass.

Decision condition: proceed with this architecture only if a repository-local prototype can demonstrate concurrent independent workers, event ordering/idempotency, interruption/replay reconciliation, redaction, snapshot rendering, and no regression in existing receipt/cursor/evidence tests. Do not infer productivity, latency, cost, or correctness improvement from Claude Code's product behavior; measure those outcomes separately.

unverifiedClaims.content:
Decision-blocking: the repository does not yet expose a production host implementation for `invokeSiblingSkill`, a worker scheduler, or a durable event store; this finding cannot establish deployment feasibility.

Decision-blocking: the exact runtime API and data structures behind Claude Code's internal dynamic workflow progress view are not public in the retrieved documentation; only its documented behavior and visible fields are treated as evidence.

Material risk: Claude Code workflow, Agent View, agent-team, hooks, streaming, and tracing features have version, provider, plan, preview, beta, or opt-in qualifications. Re-verify availability before depending on any one product surface.

Material risk: context isolation does not prove filesystem, process, network, credential, or security isolation. A CSM implementation needs independent enforcement evidence for each boundary.

Material risk: workflow replay can repeat side effects. The need for idempotency, durable markers, and at-least-once handling is an architectural inference, not a documented Claude Code guarantee.

Material risk: token totals, elapsed time, agent counts, recent tool calls, summaries, and heartbeat age are activity signals. No retrieved source establishes exact completion percentage, reliable ETA, or quality from those signals.

Informational: current local trace and journal schemas may be intentionally retrospective; the absence statements in this finding mean no live worker wiring was found in the inspected files, not that no external host can provide it.

Unverifiable: claims that dynamic workers will improve productivity, cost, latency, autonomy, quality, or user trust without controlled repository-local experiments.

processAppendix.content:
Triage: DEEP, hybrid. The question can change the architecture of the skill suite and requires both current external product behavior and a complete local skill/runtime comparison.

Research tracks: (1) csm-orchestrate runtime and protocol gaps; (2) all-skill lifecycle, adaptive decomposition, and artifact contracts; (3) local progress, trace, journal, and rendering observability; (4) current Claude Code dynamic workflows, subagents, teams, Agent View, hooks, and messaging; (5) Anthropic agent-runtime guidance, SDK loop, replay, limits, and telemetry. Five independent read-only researchers returned claim-level evidence.

Synthesis: distinguished fixed workflows, model-directed agents, dynamic script workflows, agent teams, lifecycle hooks, and observability surfaces. Local findings were mapped to the shared orchestrator and to skill-specific policies. Recommendations are labeled as inference rather than vendor fact.

Challenge: the first independent challenger downgraded unsupported isolation wording, hook/OTel conflation, and local comparative claims. It required explicit caveats for context versus security isolation, redacted telemetry, and direct local locators.

First judge: factual accuracy 0.82, citation accuracy 0.74, completeness 0.66, clarity 0.88; FAIL because context isolation, replay/idempotency, activity-versus-progress, feature status, and failure semantics were not explicit enough.

Remediation: added K12-K15, separated activity from progress and evidence, qualified preview/beta/opt-in status, made replay safety an inference, and added local line-level citations.

Second challenge: upheld the revised additions with qualifications and required stating that workflow-spawned workers' security boundary is not established by context isolation alone.

Second judge: factual accuracy 0.90, citation accuracy 0.88, completeness 0.82, clarity 0.90; PASS. Remaining corrections applied: local absence is phrased as not found in inspected files; recommendations are explicitly inferential; K4/K7/K13/K15 carry status and evidence qualifications.

Verification: all eight fixed section keys are present in required order; every claim citation resolves to a reference; journal sequences are contiguous; no declared artifacts exist; no credentials, tokens, private keys, or personal data are included. Protected repository baseline before and after research was ` M csm-autoresearch/test/runtime.test.mjs`; this pre-existing unrelated modification was not changed. The finding is the only intended persistent write from this run.
